oneLineAnswer: A prescription anticonvulsant for some seizures, facial nerve pain and bipolar mania, with rare serious skin and blood risks.
whatItIs: Carbamazepine is a prescription-only anticonvulsant medicine, sold under names such as Tegretol, Carbatrol and Equetro. Its chemical name is 5H-dibenz[b,f]azepine-5-carboxamide, and its formula is C15H12N2O with a molecular weight of 236.27. The drug substance is a white to off-white powder that barely dissolves in water.
whatItDoes: Carbamazepine is an anticonvulsant, meaning a medicine used to calm the abnormal brain activity behind seizures.
Its label lists it for complex partial seizures, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and mixed patterns combining them.
The label says it does not appear to control absence seizures, a different seizure type.
It is also used for the stabbing facial pain of true trigeminal neuralgia, a nerve pain condition.
For trigeminal neuralgia, NINDS describes anticonvulsant medicines as able to reduce how often attacks happen.
howPeopleUseIt: It comes as tablets, chewable tablets, long-acting tablets and capsules, and a liquid suspension.
It is taken by mouth for long stretches of time, often as the only medicine or alongside others.
The label warns that stopping an anticonvulsant suddenly can bring seizures back.
Before starting, doctors usually check blood counts, and some people are offered a gene test for HLA-B*1502.
The label states this drug is not a simple painkiller and should not be used for everyday aches.

commonSideEffects: The most frequently reported problems are dizziness, drowsiness, unsteadiness, nausea, and vomiting.
Those effects tend to be worst in the first weeks of treatment, according to the label.
Blurred vision, double vision, headache, and tiredness are also listed.
Dry mouth, constipation, or diarrhea can occur.
Low blood sodium, called hyponatremia, is listed among reported side effects.
seriousSigns: A rash can be the first sign of Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis, two dangerous skin reactions.
The label says to stop the drug at the first sign of a rash unless a doctor says it is unrelated.
Those skin reactions are rare but can be fatal, and most appear within the first months of use.
Fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, or easy bruising can point to a fall in blood cells.
Aplastic anemia (bone marrow making too few blood cells) and agranulocytosis (very low infection-fighting white cells) are linked to the drug.
Fever with a widespread rash and swollen lymph nodes may be DRESS, a whole-body reaction that can be life-threatening.
The label tells patients to report swelling of the face, eyes, lips, or tongue, or trouble swallowing or breathing, right away.
Antiseizure medicines including this one may raise the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior.
Yellowing of the skin or eyes, or dark urine, can signal liver injury; hepatitis and rare liver failure are listed.
whoShouldAvoid: People who have had bone marrow depression, meaning their bone marrow struggled to make blood cells.
People allergic to carbamazepine or sensitive to tricyclic drugs such as amitriptyline and imipramine.
People who test positive for the inherited gene variant HLA-B*1502, unless the benefit clearly outweighs the risk.
People taking nefazodone or delavirdine, two drugs the labels say must not be combined with carbamazepine.
People taking an MAO inhibitor, which the label says should be stopped at least 14 days before carbamazepine starts.

interactions: Carbamazepine is a strong inducer of the liver enzyme CYP3A4, so it can push levels of many other medicines down.
Some antibiotics and antifungals, such as erythromycin and ketoconazole, can raise carbamazepine levels in the body.
Grapefruit juice is named in the label as something that can increase carbamazepine levels.
Some seizure and tuberculosis medicines, including phenytoin, phenobarbital and rifampin, can lower carbamazepine levels.
Valproic acid and certain antipsychotics need extra level checks when used with carbamazepine.
The labels single out nefazodone and delavirdine as combinations that must be avoided.
Because levels shift, the label says doctors should monitor blood levels closely and adjust doses of the other medicines.
pregnancyAndChildren: Labels state that carbamazepine can harm a fetus. They report that data suggest a link between use in pregnancy and congenital malformations, including spina bifida, and that craniofacial defects, heart malformations, other anomalies, and developmental delays have also been reported. The manufacturer says the decision to use it during pregnancy should weigh benefits against risks, and that a patient who becomes pregnant should be told about the potential hazard. The liquid form contains propylene glycol, which the label carries its own warning about. Child-friendly forms, including chewable tablets and a suspension, exist for people who cannot swallow tablets.
whatWeDoNotKnow: No one knows exactly how carbamazepine works; the label itself states the mechanism of action remains unknown.
Whether the main breakdown product of the drug adds meaningful benefit or risk has not been established.
The true rate of mild drops in blood cells is unknown, and the label says data cannot estimate it accurately.
The label says the role of dose, other medicines, other illnesses and monitoring in serious skin reactions has not been studied.
The pregnancy findings are described as associations in data, not proven cause and effect.
ClinicalTrials.gov lists 262 studies that mention carbamazepine, but that count says nothing about how well it works.
Trigeminal neuralgia itself can be hard to diagnose, and in some cases no cause is found.

gaps: The NCCIH carbamazepine page returned a 404, so no NCCIH content was used.

The LiverTox carbamazepine chapter on NCBI Bookshelf (NBK548097) was blocked by a reCAPTCHA wall, so no detailed drug-induced liver injury profile was included; the liver facts above come only from the product labels.
A second Bookshelf fetch and an accessdata FDA PDF fetch failed to yield readable text (the PDF came back as raw binary), so neither was cited.
MedlinePlus drug monograph pages (medlineplus.gov/druginfo/meds/*) are excluded as ASHP-copyrighted content. One such page was loaded during source checking; no claim in this record comes from it.
One attempted DailyMed URL used a setid that does not exist and returned no content.
No grounded breastfeeding or lactation guidance appeared in the fetched labels, so it is omitted.
No grounded information was found on how carbamazepine affects children differently from adults, beyond available child-friendly dose forms.
No dose, amount, or personal schedule is recorded here by design; only label and study observations are reported.
The ClinicalTrials.gov figure is a registry count of studies mentioning the drug, not a measure of benefit.
summary: This record covers what carbamazepine is, what its labels say it is used for, its common and serious risks, its drug interactions, and its pregnancy cautions.
